      Docker for DevOps Engineers: A Complete Beginner's Guide

      Everything you need to know about containers, from writing your first Dockerfile to multi-stage builds and Docker Compose.

      🐳 Docker 📅 15 Jan 2026 ✎ Updated 18 Oct 2026 ⏱ 3 min read 📶 Beginner
      DockerContainersBeginner

      Docker changed how we build, ship, and run software. Before containers, "it works on my machine" was a real, painful problem. Docker solved it by packaging your application and everything it needs — runtime, libraries, config — into a single portable unit called a container.

      This guide walks you through Docker from scratch: what it is, why it matters, and how to write your first Dockerfile and ship a real application.

      What is Docker?

      Docker is a platform that allows you to package applications into containers. A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software — code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings.

      Key insight: Containers share the host OS kernel but run in isolated user spaces. This makes them far lighter than VMs — a container starts in milliseconds, not minutes.

      Core Docker Concepts

      Images vs Containers

      An image is a read-only blueprint — like a class in programming. A container is a running instance of that image — like an object. One image can run as many containers as you need.

      Dockerfile

      A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions to build a Docker image. Here's a real example for a Node.js app:

      # Use official Node.js image as base
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency files first (for layer caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

      Key Dockerfile Instructions

      • FROM — base image to start from
      • WORKDIR — set working directory inside the container
      • COPY — copy files from host to container
      • RUN — execute a command during build
      • EXPOSE — document which port the app uses
      • CMD — command to run when container starts
      • ENV — set environment variables

      Essential Docker Commands

      # Build an image from Dockerfile
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

# Run a container
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name myapp myapp:1.0

# List running containers
docker ps

# View container logs
docker logs myapp -f

# Stop and remove container
docker stop myapp && docker rm myapp

# List images
docker images

# Remove unused resources
docker system prune

      Multi-Stage Builds (Production Best Practice)

      Multi-stage builds let you use a large build image (with compilers and dev tools) but produce a tiny final image with only what's needed to run:

      # Stage 1: Build
FROM golang:1.23 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o myapp .

# Stage 2: Run (tiny final image)
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY --from=builder /app/myapp /myapp
CMD ["/myapp"]

      Result: The Go build image is ~800MB. The final Alpine image is ~10MB. Multi-stage builds are essential for production.

      Docker Compose

      For applications with multiple services (app + database + cache), use Docker Compose:

      # compose.yaml (the top-level "version:" key is obsolete and can be omitted)
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  pgdata:

      Run everything with a single command: docker compose up -d
